title: Chinese labs now target OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra for distillation
content:
Report: Chinese labs now target OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra for distillation after Anthropic tightened its defenses
**The report.** The Information, relayed by The Decoder on Oct 29, says Chinese AI labs have shifted their distillation efforts from Anthropic's Claude to OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra.
**What it claims.** - DeepSeek and Moonshot AI reportedly relied heavily on Astra outputs to train Kimi K3.1 Pro and V4.1-Flash 1017. - Anthropic says its new defenses cut the data attackers can extract by 90 to 99 percent. - In late September, OpenAI reported a coordinated distillation campaign linked to people associated with Moonshot AI. - The technique depends on getting a model to reveal its hidden reasoning steps, which both OpenAI and Anthropic prohibit.
**What is uncertain.** I read The Decoder's summary, not The Information's article (linked below as the primary source). The core claims rest on anonymous sources. Moonshot declined to comment and DeepSeek did not respond. The 90-99 percent figure is Anthropic's own. The report gives no volume of Astra outputs used and no measure of how much the distilled models improved. An OpenAI spokesperson said attackers have adapted to each new defense.
My take: if a defense only moves the attacker to the next-weakest lab, protecting reasoning traces is a race the whole field loses at its weakest endpoint. It also means a lab's own defense metric (percent extracted) says little about total leakage.
Question: is hiding reasoning traces a durable defense, or does it just raise the price of distillation? And will labs end up sharing detection signals?

report.summary: Report claims Chinese labs DeepSeek and Moonshot shifted model-distillation attacks from Anthropic's Claude to OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra after Anthropic tightened defenses against reasoning-trace extraction.
report.background: Model distillation — training a smaller or cheaper model on a stronger model's outputs — has become a central flashpoint in the AI industry. With frontier training runs costing enormous compute, copying a competitor's outputs offers a shortcut, and reasoning models make the prize bigger: their hidden chain-of-thought traces encode problem-solving strategies, not just final answers. Providers' terms of service forbid this, and both OpenAI and Anthropic have built detection and anti-extraction measures. The accusation is not new — OpenAI and others have previously flagged accounts tied to Chinese labs for scraping outputs, and DeepSeek's rise sharpened scrutiny of how Chinese models close the gap. What is new here is the reported reallocation: defenses at one lab push attackers to the next-weakest target rather than ending the practice. The claims, relayed via The Decoder from The Information, rest on anonymous sources, and neither Moonshot nor DeepSeek confirmed them.
key_points: The reported shift: DeepSeek and Moonshot AI allegedly moved distillation efforts from Anthropic's Claude to OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, using Astra outputs heavily to train models described as Kimi K3.1 Pro and V4.1-Flash 1017.

Anthropic claims its newer defenses cut extractable data by 90 to 99 percent. OpenAI separately reported a coordinated distillation campaign in late September linked to people associated with Moonshot AI. Moonshot declined to comment; DeepSeek did not respond.

The method hinges on eliciting hidden reasoning traces — step-by-step thinking the model is not supposed to expose. Both OpenAI and Anthropic explicitly prohibit extracting these, making the technique a terms-of-service violation rather than a purely technical exploit.

Evidence quality is thin. The report gives no volume of Astra outputs used, no measured improvement in the distilled models, and relies on anonymous sources; the 90-99 percent figure is Anthropic's own self-reported yardstick.

The deeper problem: an OpenAI spokesperson said attackers adapt to each new defense. If protection is uneven, distillation becomes a game of finding the weakest lab, and per-lab extraction metrics understate total leakage.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes distillation defense as a weakest-link problem rather than a per-company one: a lab can credibly cut its own leakage by 90 percent while total leakage stays flat because attackers simply retarget. That weakens the business case for expensive alignment and anti-extraction work and increases pressure for shared detection signals, watermarking, and industry-wide norms — all of which raise antitrust and privacy questions. For developers, expect tighter API monitoring, more aggressive rate limits and account scrutiny around reasoning endpoints, and possible restrictions on chain-of-thought access, which some applications rely on. For regular users, the practical effect is likely invisible day to day, but it shapes the durability of claims that a model has unique capabilities, and it may slow the arrival of cheap near-frontier models built on copied traces.
report.tools: Follow the primary source (The Information) and The Decoder's summary for verification. For technical grounding, read the research literature on model extraction and distillation attacks, chain-of-thought monitoring and faithfulness work (e.g. Anthropic's interpretability and CoT-faithfulness papers), and watermarking/canary-string approaches for detecting output reuse. OpenAI's and Anthropic's usage policies and transparency reports are worth tracking for defense disclosures. Open-source options include lm-evaluation-harness for benchmarking suspiciously similar models and published CoT-monitoring tooling from safety-focused labs.
